newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen steady at open, awaits Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen steady at open, awaits Greenspan.

text.p: Wall Street is expected to open steady to slightly firmer on Tuesday, as both stock and bond markets bided time until a key speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan later in the day.

The Fed chief's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to the U.S. Congress, which starts at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, will take center stage in markets while investors digested earnings from major companies like International Business Machines Corp, analysts said.

"All eyes are focused on the Greenspan testimony and earnings reports which are coming out," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said. "We have results from IBM, which is a little soft in Europe, but the main focus is on Treasury markets and Greenspan's comments."
Greenspan will deliver the mandatory semi-annual testimony on the economy and monetary policy before Congress on both Tuesday and Wednesday.
Bonds and stocks were waiting on what Greenspan would say about inflation and the stock valuations, analysts said.
"The market is looking to see if he says anything about inflation risk having diminished since March," Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics, said.
Ellis said Greenspan would not try to knock down the stock market, but that markets might end up with the impression he felt the share prices were too high.
Cardillo said Greenspan would probably not discuss the stock market, but would reiterate that the Federal Reserve would be vigilant about combatting signs of inflation.

Most stocks should trade in a narrow range ahead of the testimony, but shares of IBM could see profit-taking after the technology company posted second quarter earnings of $1.46 per share compared to $1.26 a share post-split in last year's second quarter, analysts said.
Results were slightly better than Wall Street estimates of $1.42 per share, but the stock had risen ahead of the results results and could weaken now, Cardillo said.
"The stock went up in anticipation of the results, so it might be a 'buy the rumor, sell the news' scenerio," he said.
Cardillo said IBM's declines might be short-lived and would probably not drag down the whole tech sector.
The Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was up 2.55 points at 920.20. The long bond rose 5/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
The dollar hovered in a narrow range against the yen in Tokyo, trading at around 116.12/17 yen. In Europe, the dollar extended gains against the mark, trading at 1.8125/30 marks.
The mark was weak amid ongoing concerns about Europe's plans for economic and monetary union.
Japan's Nikkei average closed down 92.30 points, or 0.46 percent, at 20,157.02.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 20.7 at 4826.4.
U.S. stocks were mixed in London trading.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that performance by money managers on average still trails the performance of the Standard & Poor's 500 index.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that First Union Corp, which plans to buy Signet Banking Corp for about $3.25 billion, might be paying a reasonable price by some measures.
